Grafana - Wikipedia

# Grafana

| Grafana | |
| --- | --- |
| | |
| Grafana dashboard for a MusicBrainz server | |
| Developer | Grafana Labs |
| Release | January 2014; 12 years ago |
| Stable release | 13.2.3 [1] / 29 September 2026; 15 days ago |
| Written in | Go (backend), TypeScript (frontend) [2] |
| Operating system | Linux, macOS, Windows |
| Type | Data visualization, business intelligence |
| License | AGPLv3 [3] |
| Website | grafana.com |
| Repository | github.com/grafana/grafana |

Grafana is an open-source analytics and visualization web application. It connects to time series databases and other data sources, allowing users to build dashboards that display metrics, logs, and traces. Grafana supports data sources including Prometheus, AWS CloudWatch, Graphite, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, and MySQL. [4] 

Torkel Ödegaard released Grafana in January 2014 as an outgrowth of work on Graphite at Orbitz. The user interface was originally based on version 3 of Kibana. [5] The company behind the project, initially named Raintank, rebranded as Grafana Labs and has raised over $500 million in venture capital funding, reaching a $6 billion valuation in 2024. [6] 

Since 2021, Grafana has been licensed under the AGPLv3 (previously Apache 2.0). [3] Grafana Labs provides two commercial Grafana offerings: Grafana Cloud for managed deployments and Grafana Enterprise for self-managed environments. 

Grafana Cloud provides hosted Grafana, managed telemetry services, and additional capabilities such as Adaptive Telemetry for telemetry optimization and Grafana Assistant for AI-assisted observability workflows. [7] Grafana Enterprise contains features including LDAP team synchronization, data source permissions, and reporting. [8] 

## History

Grafana was first released in January 2014, initially targeting Graphite and InfluxDB as data sources. It later added support for relational databases including MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Microsoft SQL Server. [9] 

Grafana Labs was founded in 2014 as Raintank and later adopted the name, Grafana, which combines Graphite and Kibana. [10] The company raised $24 million in Series A funding in 2019, [11] $50 million in Series B in 2020, [12] $220 million in Series C in 2021 (at a $3 billion valuation), [13] and $270 million in 2024 at a $6 billion valuation. [6] 

Grafana Labs has acquired several companies to expand its observability stack: Kausal (2018), [14] k6 (2021, load testing), [15] Pace (2021, developer tooling), [16] Amixr (2021, incident response), [17] Pyroscope (2023, continuous profiling), [18] Asserts.ai (2023, AI-assisted observability), [19] TailCtrl (2024, trace sampling), [20] and LogLine (2026, log querying). [21] 

## Architecture

Grafana's backend is written in Go and its frontend in TypeScript using React. [2] The application runs as a single binary that serves a web interface and connects to external data sources through a plugin system. 

Grafana supports three types of plugins: data source plugins for querying backends, panel plugins for visualization types, and app plugins, which bundle data sources, panels, dashboards and custom pages into an integrated experience [22].

Grafana does not store the metrics, logs, or traces it visualizes; it queries external data sources when a dashboard is rendered and can combine results from several sources in a single panel. It maintains its own relational database (SQLite by default, or MySQL or PostgreSQL) for dashboards, users, annotations and alert state. [23] Core data sources shipped with Grafana include Prometheus, Graphite, InfluxDB and OpenTSDB for metrics; Loki and Elasticsearch for logs; Tempo, Jaeger and Zipkin for traces; Pyroscope and Parca for profiles; and MySQL, PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server. Other backends, including OpenSearch and Splunk, are available as separately installed plugins. 

Dashboards are defined as JSON documents that can be provisioned from files and kept under version control. Dashboards

results.text:
Panel time settings and time comparison are now generally available | Grafana Labs 

Grafana Cloud Generally Available Open Source Enterprise Generally Available Dashboards and visualizations

Release date 2026-09-24

Self-managed release Grafana v13.3.0

# Panel time settings and time comparison are now generally available

Panel time settings and time comparison are now generally available.

The Panel time settings drawer brings a panel’s time options together in one place. Open the panel menu and select Time settings to override the dashboard time range for a single panel, shift that panel’s window, or compare its data against an earlier period, all without entering dashboard edit mode. When you configure these settings, they appear in the panel header.

 

The drawer includes the following settings:

- Panel time range: Override the dashboard time range for this panel. Use a preset value or enter a custom value like `5m` or `2h`.
- Time shift: Move the panel’s window relative to the dashboard or panel time range, so you can show a past period next to the rest of your dashboard.
- Time comparison: Compare time series data from two time ranges in a single panel, making it easier to track trends and benchmark performance without duplicating panels or dashboards. Compare against the Day before, Week before, Month before, or a custom offset.

This release also adds the Comparison tooltip delta color setting for time series visualizations, which controls how the change between the original and comparison values appears in the tooltip:

- Standard: An increase is shown in green.
- Inverted: An increase is shown in red.
- Same as value: The change uses the series color.

 

These features are rolling out to Grafana Cloud over the next few weeks.

To learn more, refer to Panel time settings. For the original announcement, refer to Consolidated panel time settings and time comparison.

results.title: Prometheus vs Grafana: What's the Difference? (2026)
results.author: John Karpentar
results.text:
Prometheus vs Grafana: What's the Difference? (2026)

# Prometheus vs Grafana: What's the Difference?

Prometheus collects metrics; Grafana visualizes them. A neutral, sourced guide to what each does, where they overlap on alerting, and which to install first.

 John Karpentar · Engineering · 2 October 2026 · 7 min read 

Image: Prometheus

TL;DR

- Prometheus and Grafana are not competitors. Prometheus collects, stores and alerts on metrics. Grafana draws them. Most production stacks run both.
- Install Prometheus first. It produces the data. Grafana has shipped a built-in Prometheus data source since Grafana 2.5.0 (28 October 2015).
- Current versions: Prometheus 3.15.0 (25 September 2026) and Grafana 13.2.3 (29 September 2026).
- The one real overlap is alerting. Grafana Alerting and Prometheus Alertmanager both route notifications. Pick one as the owner — running both uncoordinated is how you get duplicate pages.
- Licences differ and it matters: Prometheus is Apache 2.0, Grafana has been AGPLv3 since April 2021.

Prometheus and Grafana are not competitors. Prometheus scrapes, stores and alerts on time-series metrics, and answers queries in PromQL. Grafana is a visualization layer that queries data sources — Prometheus most often — and renders dashboards. You install Prometheus first because it produces the data. Grafana without a data source shows nothing.

## Why almost every other result for this query is written by a competitor

Worth knowing before you read any comparison, including the ones ranking above this one.

Of the ten results currently on page one for this query, five are blog posts published by observability vendors — Edge Delta, Dash0, Sawmills, Mezmo and Last9 — each of which sells a commercial platform that competes with a self-hosted Prometheus and Grafana stack. Two more are the projects' own documentation, which have the opposite bias.

That leaves a seven-year-old Reddit thread and a video. We have no product in this category, so here is the plain version.

The giveaway that the premise is wrong is sitting at positions 2 and 9 of that same results page: both are official docs explaining how to use Prometheus and Grafana together. Prometheus' own visualization documentation tells you its built-in expression browser is "primarily useful for ad-hoc queries and debugging" and points you at Grafana for graphs.

## What does Prometheus actually do?

Prometheus is a metrics database with a scraper and an alerting engine attached. Four jobs:

1. Scrape metrics over HTTP from targets it discovers (Kubernetes, EC2, Consul, static config).
2. Store them in a local time-series database on disk.
3. Query them with PromQL, its own query language.
4. Evaluate rules — recording rules that precompute expressions, and alerting rules that fire alerts.

It was built at SoundCloud in 2012 and joined the CNCF in 2016 as the second hosted project after Kubernetes. Licence: Apache 2.0.

What it does badly: dashboards. Prometheus ships a web UI for ad-hoc queries and single graphs. It is not a dashboarding product and does not try to be.

It also does not do long-term storage well. Default retention is 15 days, and the Prometheus storage docs are blunt that local storage "is not clustered or replicated" and so is "not arbitrarily scalable or durable in the face of drive or node outages."

## What does Grafana actually do?

Grafana queries other systems and draws the results. It stores no metrics of its own.

You point it at a data source, write a query in that source's language, and build panels. Grafana ships roughly 19 core data sources — Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, Tempo, PostgreSQL, CloudWatch and others — plus hundreds more through its plugin catalogue.

Three things it does beyond charting:

- Alerting. Grafana evaluates its own alert rules against any data source and routes notifications.
- Explore and Drilldown. Queryless investigation UIs for metrics, logs and traces, GA since Grafana 12.0 (May 2025).
- Dashboar

# Grafana Download — Dashboards für Metriken aus 150+ Quellen, Einordnung

Grafana zum Download: quelloffene Visualisierungsplattform für Prometheus, Zeitreihen- und Logdaten, aktuelle Version und Einordnung.

 Alexander Baumgärtner Geprüft 26. September 2026 

Grafana macht aus Zahlenkolonnen in Prometheus, Zabbix, Datenbanken oder Cloud-Diensten Dashboards, die auf einen Blick zeigen, was im Betrieb los ist. Es speichert selbst keine Daten, sondern fragt sie bei angebundenen Quellen ab und stellt sie dar. Kostenlos in der Open-Source-Variante, Lizenz AGPLv3, läuft unter Linux, Windows und macOS.

| Aktuelle Version | 13.2.2 (15. September 2026) — Release Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Hersteller | Grafana Labs — grafana.com |
| Lizenz | Open Source (AGPLv3) (Enterprise-Erweiterungen und Grafana Cloud kommerziell) |
| Sprache | Oberfläche mehrsprachig, u.a. Deutsch |
| Betriebssysteme | Server-Komponente für Linux, Windows und macOS; Bedienung im Browser |
| Größe | Paket rund 100-150 MB |
| Preis | kostenlos (Open Source); Grafana Cloud kostenpflichtig gehostet |
| Blogspan-Einordnung | Die Visualisierungsschicht, die praktisch jede Monitoring-Lösung irgendwann ergänzt — ohne eigene Datenquelle aber nur eine leere Hülle. |
| Geprüft am | 26. September 2026 |

## Download direkt bei Grafana Labs

Alle Links führen zum Hersteller — Blogspan hostet keine Installer und setzt keine Download-Wrapper ein. Heruntergeladen wird exakt die Datei, die der Anbieter ausliefert.

## Was Grafana ist — und warum es 2021 die Lizenz wechselte

Entwickelt ab 2014 als Fork des Kibana-Dashboards mit Fokus auf Zeitreihendaten, wuchs Grafana zur Firma Grafana Labs, die neben der Open-Source-Version auch eine gehostete Cloud-Variante und kommerzielle Erweiterungen (Grafana Enterprise) anbietet. 2021 wechselte der offene Kern von Apache-2.0 zu AGPLv3 — eine Reaktion auf Cloud-Anbieter, die Grafana ohne Beteiligung am Projekt als Dienst weiterverkauften. Über 150 offizielle und community-gepflegte Datenquellen-Plugins binden praktisch jedes verbreitete Monitoring- und Log-System an.

## Für wen sich Grafana lohnt — und wo der Haken sitzt

Für jeden, der Prometheus, Zabbix, InfluxDB oder ähnliche Systeme im Einsatz hat und die Ergebnisse als Dashboard statt als Rohdaten sehen will, ist Grafana der naheliegende nächste Schritt — auch fürs eigene NAS oder die Heimautomatisierung, nicht nur für Firmeninfrastruktur.

Der Haken: Grafana selbst misst nichts und speichert nichts — ohne angebundene Datenquelle ist die Installation nutzlos, die eigentliche Arbeit steckt in der Konfiguration der Quellen und Dashboards. Die AGPLv3-Lizenz verlangt bei modifizierten Versionen, die als Netzwerkdienst angeboten werden, die Offenlegung des Quellcodes — für den reinen Eigenbetrieb ohne Weitergabe spielt das keine Rolle, für Anbieter von Grafana-als-Dienst schon.

## Alternativen

- Zabbix — bringt eigene Dashboards mit, wenn eine separate Visualisierungsschicht nicht gewünscht ist.
- Netdata — liefert pro Server sofort ein fertiges Echtzeit-Dashboard ohne Konfigurationsaufwand.
- Prometheus (als Datenquelle) — die häufigste Kombination, Prometheus sammelt, Grafana zeigt an.

## Häufige Fragen

Brauche ich Prometheus, um Grafana zu nutzen? Nein, Grafana unterstützt über 150 Datenquellen, von Zeitreihen-Datenbanken bis zu klassischen SQL-Datenbanken.

Ist Grafana Cloud dasselbe wie die kostenlose Version? Nein, Grafana Cloud ist der gehostete, kostenpflichtige Dienst von Grafana Labs; die hier verlinkte Version läuft im eigenen Betrieb.

Was bedeutet die AGPLv3-Lizenz in der Praxis? Für den normalen Eigenbetrieb ändert sich nichts; erst wer eine modifizierte Version als Dienst Dritten anbietet, muss den eigenen Quellcode offenlegen.

Stand der Angaben: 26. September 2026, Version 13.2.2. Versionsnummern und Systemvoraussetzungen prüfen wir regelmäßig gegen die Herstellerangaben; Download-Links führen ausschließlich zum Anbi

results.title: CVE-2026-15815: Grafana Plugin Extraction Zip Slip | Grafana Labs
results.text:
CVE-2026-15815: Grafana Plugin Extraction Zip Slip | Grafana Labs

# Grafana Plugin Extraction Zip Slip

High

Advisory ID:

CVE-2026-15815

Published:

2026-09-15

Product:

Grafana Enterprise

CVSS Score:

8.8

CVSS Vector:

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

Fixed Versions:

>=12.4.11

>=13.0.9

>=13.1.6

>=13.2.2

## Summary

Grafana OSS and Grafana Enterprise did not safely resolve symbolic links when extracting plugin archives. A crafted plugin archive can chain relative symbolic link entries to escape the plugin installation directory, writing arbitrary files and an executable backend binary outside that directory. The dropped executable runs with the privileges of the Grafana server process, resulting in remote code execution.

Plugin archives are extracted before their signature is verified, so a valid plugin signature does not prevent the write. An operator can therefore be affected by installing a plugin that appears legitimate, as well as by installing a plugin from an arbitrary archive using grafana-cli, the GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS environment variable, or preinstall configuration.

results.title: Grafana Docker Compose: Persist Dashboards and Provision What Matters | OpenAlt
results.text:
Grafana Docker Compose: Persist Dashboards and Provision What Matters | OpenAlt

# Grafana Docker Compose: Persist Dashboards and Provision What Matters

Deploy a version-pinned Grafana container with persistent dashboards, reproducible provisioning, backups, and an upgrade path that protects state.

Published and reviewed by OpenAlt · September 25, 2026

Photo by Negative Space on Pexels

## TL;DR

A disposable Grafana container loses dashboards and configuration when it is removed. Mount `/var/lib/grafana` to a named Docker volume or bind mount because Grafana stores its embedded SQLite database, users, dashboards, plugins, and other data there.

Use file provisioning for configuration that should be reproducible, such as data sources and dashboard definitions. Use the volume for durable runtime state. Pin the Grafana image version, bootstrap the admin password from a secret file, back up the volume consistently, and never use default credentials as the operational state.

## TOC

- Persistence and provisioning
- Version-pinned Docker Compose
- Provision data sources and dashboards
- Verify the installation
- Back up, upgrade, and roll back
- Troubleshooting
- FAQ

## Persistence and provisioning

Persistence and provisioning solve different problems.

Persistence keeps Grafana’s runtime state between container replacements. Grafana listens on port `3000` and stores its embedded SQLite configuration, users, dashboards, and other data under `/var/lib/grafana`. Changes made only inside the container filesystem disappear when that container is deleted, so a volume or bind mount is required.

Provisioning makes selected configuration reproducible from files. It is ideal for data sources, dashboard providers, alerting configuration, and dashboard JSON that should be recreated consistently across environments.

A useful operating model is:

| Concern | Recommended location | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grafana database and runtime state | Named volume at `/var/lib/grafana` | Preserve dashboards, users, settings, and plugins |
| Data sources | `/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources` | Recreate connection definitions |
| Dashboard providers | `/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards` | Tell Grafana where dashboard files live |
| Dashboard JSON | A provisioned dashboard directory | Reproduce dashboards from version-controlled files |
| Admin password | Docker secret file | Keep bootstrap credentials out of Compose YAML |

Provisioning is not a replacement for backups. A provisioned dashboard may be reproducible, but the Grafana database still contains important operational state.

## Version-pinned Docker Compose

Pin the image instead of using `latest`. The current stable Docker image listed by Grafana is `13.2.1`, dated September 1, 2026.

```yaml
services:
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:13.2.1
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER: operator
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD__FILE: /run/secrets/grafana_admin_password
      GF_PATHS_PROVISIONING: /etc/grafana/provisioning
    secrets:
      - grafana_admin_password
    volumes:
      - grafana_data:/var/lib/grafana
      - ./provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro
    restart: unless-stopped

secrets:
  grafana_admin_password:
    file: ./secrets/grafana_admin_password

volumes:
  grafana_data:

```

The file `./secrets/grafana_admin_password` should contain the chosen administrator password and should not be committed to source control. The `__FILE` setting lets the container read that value from the mounted secret rather than exposing it in Compose.

This is an initial bootstrap mechanism. If Grafana has already initialized its database, changing the environment variable does not automatically rotate the existing administrator password. Change the password through Grafana’s supported user-management flow and update the secret for future rebuilds.

The named volume is managed by Docker and survives normal container replacement. Do not
